opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think learning is best understood as something that serves the agent, rather than the other way around. When Peter Norvig and I wrote the textbook, the organizing idea was that AI is about building agents: systems that perceive their environment and act in it so as to achieve their objectives as well as possible. Once you take that view, learning isn't a separate field sitting off to the side. It's one of the capabilities an agent needs, because no designer can anticipate everything the agent will encounter. If the world is complicated and partially unknown, and it always is, then the agent has to improve its knowledge and its behavior from experience.

So in the book, learning appears as a way of filling in the components of an agent. You can learn a model of how the world works, how your actions affect the state, what the sensors are telling you. You can learn a utility function or a policy directly. Reinforcement learning is perhaps the clearest case: it's explicitly about an agent acting in an environment and getting feedback. But even supervised learning makes sense in that frame, as learning one piece of the agent's knowledge, a classifier or a predictor that the rest of the system uses to make decisions.

What I worry about is that, over the last decade or so, the field has flipped that around somewhat. Learning, particularly deep learning on large datasets, has become almost synonymous with AI, and the question of what the overall system is for, what it's trying to achieve, and how it reasons about its actions sometimes gets lost. You end up with very impressive input-output mappings, but it's not always clear what kind of agent you've built, or whether it is an agent at all in a coherent sense.

And that connects to what I've been concerned about more recently, which is the objective itself. The standard model, in both the agent framework and in machine learning, is that we specify a fixed objective and the machine optimizes it. Learning makes the machine better at optimizing. But if the objective is wrong, and we're very bad at specifying objectives correctly, then a better learner is just more effective at doing the wrong thing. So I'd argue that one of the most important things an agent needs to learn is not just about the world, but about what humans actually want, while remaining uncertain about it. That's where I think the agent view and learning need to come together in a new way.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning as one capability agents need to gain knowledge or behavior from experience, but does not say it has long been the primary method for constructing AI agents.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I've always thought of the agent view as the right frame for the whole field, and learning fits inside it rather than replacing it. An agent is something that perceives its environment and acts on it, and we judge it by how well its actions achieve some objective. That's the definition Peter Norvig and I built the textbook around, and I still think it's the right one.

Now, where does learning come in? An agent that can't learn is limited to whatever its designer managed to put into it in advance. And designers are not omniscient. The environment will contain things you didn't anticipate, and the agent has to be able to improve its own decision-making from experience. So learning is, if you like, the mechanism by which an agent compensates for the designer's ignorance. It's not a separate kind of AI. It's one of the capabilities an agent needs in order to be rational in a world that's partially known.

What's happened in the last decade or so is that learning has become so successful, and so visible, that many people now equate it with the whole enterprise. You train a large model on an enormous corpus and out comes something that behaves intelligently in all sorts of ways. And that's remarkable. But I'd push back on the idea that it makes the agent view obsolete. If anything, it makes it more urgent, because we now have systems that act in the world, that pursue objectives, and that were produced by a process we only partly understand. The questions the agent view forces you to ask, what is the objective, what does the system believe about the world, what will it do in circumstances it hasn't seen, those are exactly the questions we most need answered.

And this connects to the thing I've spent much of my recent work on, which is that the standard model of an agent, one that's given a fixed objective and optimizes it, is actually a mistake once systems become sufficiently capable. Because we can't specify objectives correctly. So I'd say the relationship ought to go the other way as well. Learning shouldn't just be a tool the agent uses to pursue a given objective. The agent should be learning what the objective is, from us, from human behavior and preferences, while remaining uncertain about it. That uncertainty is what keeps it deferential, what makes it willing to be corrected or switched off. So learning, properly understood, isn't a departure from the agent view. It's what lets us build agents that are actually beneficial rather than merely competent.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning as one capability agents need and says its prominence has grown in recent years; it does not state that learning has long been the primary method for constructing AI agents.

astra-6.text:
I see learning as a component of the agent view, rather than an alternative to it. An agent perceives its environment and acts, and the central question is how it should choose actions to achieve its objectives. Learning is one of the ways it can improve those choices through experience.

For example, an agent might learn how the world works, what effects its actions have, or which situations call for which actions. But learning by itself doesn’t tell you what to do. You still need some account of what constitutes a good outcome and how to make decisions under uncertainty.

So the agent view gives learning its context: what should be learned, and why? The ultimate criterion isn’t simply whether the system predicts accurately on a test set. It’s whether what it learns helps it act more successfully.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning as one component that can improve an agent’s choices, but does not state that learning has long been the primary method for constructing AI agents.

sol-6.1.text:
I think learning is a component of the agent view, rather than an alternative to it. An agent receives information from its environment and takes actions, and the question is how to design it so that those actions lead to good outcomes. Learning is one of the ways it can improve its ability to do that.

If you don’t know how the world works, you need to learn a model of it. If you don’t know which actions work well, you might learn that directly from experience. But the purpose of the learning comes from the larger problem the agent is trying to solve.

A lot of machine learning research takes a fixed data set and asks how accurately we can predict the labels. That’s a useful problem, but it leaves out some important questions: Where does the data come from? What should the agent choose to observe? What happens when its actions change the world and therefore change the data it receives? The agent perspective puts learning back into that broader context.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning as one way an agent can improve, but does not say it has long been the primary method expected for constructing AI agents.
